title: Growing holy
hookLine: grace keeps growing a person; John Wesley even spoke of being made perfect in love

cards: "But grow in grace." They sit near the end of the second letter of Peter, and take something for granted. The readers already belong to God, and they're still unfinished.

A kid who knows she's loved at home still has to learn to share the last cookie, to say sorry first, to tell the truth when a lie would be quicker. Being loved doesn't end the growing. It's where the growing starts.
An English preacher named John Wesley, whose followers became the Methodists, pushed that growth a long way: he spoke of a heart made perfect in love.

teach.b: Start with the word holy. In the Bible, holy often means set apart, belonging to God, the way a cup set aside for the altar is no longer just a kitchen cup.
Paul writes to the Thessalonians: "For this is the will of God, even your sanctification." So it's two things at once. You're set apart.

teach.h: SET APART, THEN GROWN INTO IT.
teach.b: Then, slowly, you become what you were set apart for. The churches picture that growth differently.
Lutheran and Reformed Christians speak of being declared right with God by faith; being made holy is the lifelong work that follows, unfinished this side of death.
Catholics speak of grace that heals and lifts, growing through the sacraments and free cooperation. The Orthodox word, theosis, pictures being drawn into God's own life. Then Wesley.
He read Jesus's words in the Sermon on the Mount, "Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect," and asked a plain question: would God command what could never happen?
His answer was what he called Christian perfection. Not a life with no mistakes: in his own account, people made perfect in love still misjudge things and still need forgiveness.
He meant a heart so full of love for God and neighbor that love runs the whole house, with no rooms kept back. Methodist and Holiness churches have taught a version of this.
Other Christians think it promises too much for this life.
Wesley leaned on yesterday's line from John: "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear."

teach.h: WESLEY: A HEART RUN BY LOVE.
teach.b: He heard a promise in it for this life.

how: Christians in many churches speak of sanctification as lifelong growth in holiness through prayer, scripture, worship and the sacraments; Methodist and Holiness churches also teach Wesley's hope of a heart made perfect in love.

s: Wesley's perfection meant a life with no mistakes
he meant a heart full of love for God and neighbor; in his account, such people still misjudge things and still need forgiveness.
Paul calls sanctification the will of God
"for this is the will of God, even your sanctification" (1 Thessalonians 4:3).
every church agrees holiness can be complete in this life
Methodist and Holiness churches have taught a version of it; Lutheran and Reformed teaching says the work isn't finished this side of death.

games.q: you're John Wesley, reading "be ye therefore perfect." what do you make of it?
o: an impossible ideal, meant only to humble us.
God commands it, so love can truly fill a heart.
a rule for monks and nuns, not ordinary people.
games.why: Wesley asked whether God would command the impossible, and taught Christian perfection: not flawlessness, but a heart run by love.

practice: Bring to mind one person you'll see soon, and choose one small thing you could do for them again and again: a real hello instead of a nod, letting them finish a sentence, a message that asks how they're actually doing.
Growth, in this picture, is less a leap than a habit watered daily. If you pray, ask for grace to keep at it; if you don't, hold the person and the habit together.

carryVoice: Your line: perfect in love. Not flawless, just full of love. Rest well.
